### 2026-10-07 – Day 1 of my first hardware adventure!!!

**1h**

Day 1 of my first hardware adventure!!!

![Zrzut ekranu_20261008_001236](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3N0PhtlfAM8tN3x4nOdCORba3rrrqYEl/22f329000c7f6bbc67feb09151265507fb5a64cf86784212b6976995a51b9b8c.png)

![Zrzut ekranu_20261008_001225](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3N0PhtlfAM8tN3x4nOdCORba3rrrqYEl/db0ea3476c1974873a8fee7dfab988d65379239ae11c82b53d675223e86b0c1b.png)

I had meant to get started about two days ago but lacked the motivation; today, however, I decided to begin, even though I was short on time. I set up a GitHub repo, installed the required footprints and symbols, and opened the schematic editor. Since this wasn't actually my very first KiCad schematic, I had a decent idea of ​​what to do (though I struggled a bit with boxes, text, and labels). I noticed a photo of the completed schematics at the very top of the guide I was using, so I thought I had to recreate it myself—which took me about an hour—only to scroll further down and realize... Anyway, I started from the back, adding two switches and connecting them to "GPI" labels on one side and GND on the other. Next, I moved to the environment sensor section: I placed a DHT11 and connected it to GND, +3.3V, and a "DHT11 DATA" label. I also added the resistor shown in the image, though I still don't actually know what it does (hopefully, I'll find out when designing the PCB). Then I moved on to the OLED, placing a `Conn_01x04_pin` connector and wiring pin 1 to GND, 2 to +3.3V, 3 to SCL, and 4 to SDA. Finally, I tackled the MPU6050; I placed a `Conn_01x08_Pin` connector and wired it almost exactly like the OLED, except I swapped the +3.3V and GND connections as shown in the guide. I’m not entirely sure why we used 8 pins when we only needed 4, but—being a complete beginner—I won’t overthink it; maybe it’s some ancient hardware rule. Next, I moved on to the ESP32: I labeled D1 as DHT11, D2 as GPIO2, D3 as GPIO3, D4 as SCL, and D5 as SDA; I connected GND to GND (who would’ve guessed, lol), VBUS to +5V, and 3V3_OUT to +3.3V. Unfortunately, I couldn't manage without AI—though it only helped me figure out which keyboard key to press to edit and place labels. That’s all for today; see you on Day 2!!!

### 2026-10-08 – Day 2

**1h**

Day 2

![Zrzut ekranu_20261008_234550](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3N0PhtlfAM8tN3x4nOdCORba3rrrqYEl/ac1d410e6819c73f50e8f1421f946438c3b9d1038c908b592986227c47cb1999.png)

![Zrzut ekranu_20261008_234604](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3N0PhtlfAM8tN3x4nOdCORba3rrrqYEl/d0c04d99b7ad44a2681546e160b7eebda5d5965b8b09f157d9aca6a878dc1c9e.png)

Today, I focused on designing the PCB itself and assigning footprints. The biggest issue I ran into was assigning the wrong footprint to a resistor, which took me a while to figure out. But to sum it up: I assigned a 4-pin connector to the screen, an 8-pin connector to the 8-pin header, the resistor to an Axial footprint, the buttons to Cherry MX switches, the DHT11 to the Aosong sensor, and the ESP32 to the imported ESP32 model. Next, I moved on to the PCB layout; I gave the shape some thought and decided on a classic Game Boy style, though I added slightly rounded corners. I’ve positioned the components—I think in the ideal spots—and tomorrow I’ll be tackling the routing (I believe that’s the term for drawing the traces). Thanks to my new graphics tablet (shoutout to Jame Gam), I created the nickname that will appear on the board, but if there’s extra space, I’ll try to add some more interesting drawings. See you tomorrow!

### 2026-10-10 – Day 3

**2h**

Day 3

![Zrzut ekranu_20261010_125114](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3N0PhtlfAM8tN3x4nOdCORba3rrrqYEl/4c15dbd42f801ff08bc258756c890a6bf4b1317b7ddc93ee0789860c42a4fbdd.png)

![Zrzut ekranu_20261010_125132](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3N0PhtlfAM8tN3x4nOdCORba3rrrqYEl/42bf656cecb2cb35fb6e3d541bec64b92f966b8d1a64844661cdd1896deb1305.png)

![Zrzut ekranu_20261010_125149](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3N0PhtlfAM8tN3x4nOdCORba3rrrqYEl/b462e340e79628b760b59fdedf2fc09c1711e13cb52df21af82c1ae3584afe96.png)

Unfortunately, I had to skip yesterday, but today I’m back to finish my project. This is the first of two posts I’ll be making today; I wanted to keep them separate rather than dumping everything in at once. In this post, I completed the rest of the PCB by routing the connections and adding graphics. The biggest challenges today were the routing itself and the copper pour for the GND plane. I lost count of how many errors popped up regarding clearances, even if I were counting on my fingers in binary, but I managed to fix them somehow. I had heard somewhere that perpendicular traces shouldn't be used, so I decided to remove them, even though I later read that this is actually a myth. I couldn't think of what to draw on the board, so I settled on my nickname with a smiley face (c:), a laptop, and a Minecraft potion bottle, which got somewhat distorted during the PNG-to-SVG conversion. I created all these graphics on a drawing tablet using Photopea and LibreSprite; I ran into some issues with image sizing in LibreSprite, but I managed to fix that eventually. So, let's get down to business; the GND connection is straightforward, so I'll skip that. I described the schematic connections in detail in the previous post, and I followed that same layout here. However, I had to route the 3.3V line on the bottom layer, which caused it to intersect with the SDA line; this meant I had to use vias for the SDA trace. I had to route the SDA line along the bottom because the SCL line was running along the top and would have otherwise crossed it. I had to do the same thing with the 3.3V line for the environmental sensor because it was crossing the DHT11 DATA line. The rest went smoothly, except for another 3.3V line, this time for the MPU6050 and OLED, where I ran into a GND issue (an isolated island was created), so I had to route it on the top layer instead of the bottom. I think that’s it. I’ll be back later with the firmware.
